title: All nine back tightening, with a split on the size of the first move
summary: All nine members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted to tighten at the meeting ending on 4 November. Eight supported a quarter-point increase from 3.75% to 4%, and Catherine Mann preferred a half-point increase to 4.25%. The minutes explain why members acted while clear wage and price feedback from more expensive energy was still limited. Energy costs had risen further, recent UK demand and activity had exceeded expectations, and disinflation in some domestic prices appeared to have stalled. Agreement on the direction of this move concealed different views on what would justify another increase (summary and paragraphs 12–23).

Over the 15 working days to 27 October, front-month Brent averaged $108 per barrel and UK gas averaged 216 pence per therm. These prices were 38% and 81% above the July Report comparison. They also exceeded that report’s adverse fourth-quarter assumptions by 5% and 27% respectively. The two comparisons have different denominators. Direct energy effects contributed around one percentage point to September’s 3.5% CPI inflation. Staff expected inflation around 4½% in the first quarter of 2027 and around 5% in the second. Renewing household and company contracts would continue to transmit higher costs even if energy followed the assumed declining futures curve (paragraphs 3–9).

The timing of price increases mattered for the vote. Companies with unexpired fixed energy contracts had some protection. Others had seen bills rise and absorbed the increase in margins. Limited price rises so far could therefore reflect weak pricing power, temporary protection or some of both. Pay and price intentions had changed little since September, yet the bills employees would see by the time of their next wage negotiation were still rising. Members also considered the risk that businesses would cut jobs or investment if higher energy and finance costs weakened cash flow. The same initial shock could generate quite different domestic pressures depending on who absorbed the loss (paragraphs 4–12 and Ramsden’s statement).

Activity associated with AI investment and exports had supported growth. Household spending held up better than expected, although confidence had weakened. Mortgage rates offered to new customers had risen almost 50 basis points since early September and approvals were falling, while business credit growth remained strong. The evidence gave members grounds to reconsider how much slack remained and how restrictive policy already was. The survey median for Bank Rate was 4% for November and 4.25% for February. It described respondents’ expectations before the decision and could not establish how investors would react to the minutes or the accompanying projections (paragraphs 9–18).

Individual statements make the next decision less mechanical than the vote count implies. Andrew Bailey and Clare Lombardelli saw a case for further near-term action if the inflation risks failed to ease. Huw Pill thought one quarter point was unlikely to suffice. Sarah Breeden wanted more evidence on whether disinflation had stalled, and Swati Dhingra stressed evidence of recovering purchasing and pricing power and feedback between wages and prices. Alan Taylor saw an insurance case for raising the rate now and a risk in extrapolating that action automatically. Mann placed greater weight on threshold effects from salient prices and the possibility of a more persistent energy shock. These were individual assessments. The collective statement committed members to examining the evidence afresh at each meeting (individual statements, pp. 5–9).

questions.question: Did the meeting surprise investors about the next hike rather than the current one?
questions.detail: Compare pre-release meeting-dated forwards and options with the survey median, preserving each observation’s date. Measure revisions to February and later contracts around the release and accompanying Report. A well-anticipated move to 4% could still change the distribution of later rates if the vote revealed more insurance demand or the projected inflation peak shifted. Intraday data alone cannot separate the simultaneous publications.

questions.question: When did firms start to pass higher energy costs on to customers?
questions.detail: Use the expiry schedule of firms’ fixed energy contracts to separate predictable increases in input costs from changes in margins and pricing power. Track sales volumes alongside product prices before and after renewal. Higher pass-through under strong demand and smaller margin compression would support a different interpretation from loss-making firms raising prices while quantities contract. Separate food, utilities and low-energy services.

questions.question: Does stronger credit growth mean that the effective monetary stance was too loose?
questions.detail: Separate new loans, drawdowns on existing facilities and changes in outstanding balances. Compare firms exposed to AI-related expansion or stronger exports with consumer-facing businesses facing squeezed margins, and compare mortgagors with different reset dates. Strong aggregate credit may reflect investment demand, higher working-capital needs or refinancing pressure. Link those flows to investment, sales and employment before interpreting them as evidence of economy-wide demand.

questions.question: Did a more visible inflation peak reach wage negotiations or only near-term household expectations?
questions.detail: Compare 2027 settlements with each employer’s earlier expectation, the CPI news between survey and negotiation and local recruitment conditions. Account for minimum-wage changes and the composition of employment. A larger settlement surprise for negotiations taking place after salient bills arrive would support the proposed feedback. A temporary rise in year-ahead household expectations alone would leave the strength of that mechanism unresolved.
